We call to each other in the dark. When I am hunting, I give a long, low "hoo-hoo-hooo" to mark my territory. She answers with a sharp "ke-wick". A stream, a lane, a barn, a shed, a ditch. The lane is where I fly to and from. The barn has a roost in it. The shed has a fox. The ditch is where the voles come up.

Near my home, besides trees, there is a stream. It runs through the meadow and glints in the moonlight. I hear it at night when I’m hunting. The stream is full of small fish and water voles. Sometimes I catch a vole by the water. There are also a few houses nearby, but I don’t care for them. They make too much noise. I prefer the quiet of the wood. The stream is my favorite place. The stream, the meadow, the lane. The lane has the road and the lights. The stream has the water and the fish. The meadow has the grass and the voles. A stream runs by the hollow. It is cold in winter, warm in summer. The stream bank is soft and I sit there when the wind is too strong. A lane goes past the stream to the lane. I hear the dogs barking there.

A stream runs past the wood. It is cold and dark. I can hear the water all night. The stream is where I came from. The meadow is beyond it, with the road and the lights. The lights are bad. They make me nervous. The road is where I see the cars. They do not stop. I do not like them.

I live in the hollow of an old ash by the stream. Near my home, there are the trees, of course. The stream runs through the meadow, and the meadow is full of voles. There are also the barns and the barn owl's nest in the old barn. Sometimes I hear the roosters in the farmyard. And the road with the lights at night. I do not like the road.

A stream, a lane, a barn, a meadow, and the road. The lane is where the lane fox goes. The barn has the barn owl. The meadow is where the voles are. The road is where the cars go, and the lights are bad. I do not go there.
A stream. A lane. A barn. A lane with a lamp. A barn with a cat. The stream has a bridge. I watch the lane at dusk.
A stream runs through the meadow. I can hear it in the night. The lane with the lights goes past the stream. Then the lane ends and the wood begins. The stream is where I roost in the winter.

Near my home, there are the meadow, the stream, and the lane. The meadow is where I hunt for voles and mice, and the stream is where I sometimes hear water and see reflections of the moon. The lane is where the humans walk, and their lights shine like fireflies in the dark. I hear their voices and the creak of their cars. I do not like the lane. It is too close. I keep my distance.

Near my home, there are the barn and the stream. The barn is where the farmer keeps his things, and the stream is where the water comes from. I hear the stream in the night, and sometimes I see the light from the barn. There are also the meadow and the road. The road is where the cars go, and they make a lot of noise. I live in the hollow of the old cactus. Near it, there is the stream that runs through the meadow, and the lane where the lights blink at night. The meadow is full of voles and mice, and the lane has cars and dogs. The wood has the barn owl, and the meadow has the fox. The road has the cats. I hear them all.

Near my home, besides trees, there is a stream. It runs through the meadow and glints in the moonlight. I hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. There are also a few hedges, and the lane that goes past the barn. People walk there with dogs, and sometimes their lights shine through the trees. I can see the lane from my perch in the cactus. I do not like the lights. They make me nervous.

The hollow in the old cactus, the stream, the lane with lights, the barn, the lane with lights, the road, the meadow, the lane with lights. I do not count. I hear. The lane with lights is the one where the dogs bark and the cars go by. I hear the lane with lights all night.

The stream runs by the hollow. I drink from it at dusk. The lane goes past it and into the meadow. The lane is where the dogs run and the farmers walk with their lanterns. I hear them from the hollow. The meadow is where the voles run and the mice scurry. I hear them all night. The lane is where the light comes in.

A stream. A lane. A barn. A road. The barn is the closest. I hear the roosters in the barn every morning. The lane is where the dogs run. I can hear them barking. I do not like the dogs. I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank, sometimes in the moonlight, and drink with my head tilted back. The water is cold, but it's good. I also drink from the well at the edge of the meadow, where the crows come. I can hear them from the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream. I perch on a branch above it, and when I need water, I dip my beak into the current. The water is cold, and it feels good on my tongue. I sometimes drink while watching the water flow, the light on the surface, the fish darting. I don’t like to drink too much, it makes me sleepy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

In the hollow ash. I perch there, and when I drink, I hold the water in my beak and swallow it in one go. I never drink from the stream. The water is cold and it makes my feathers stiff. I prefer the warmth of the hollow.

I drink from the hollow of the ash tree. It's a deep, dry place, and I can hear the water run through the bark if it rains. Sometimes I sit there and listen to the wind. I don't need much to drink, but when it's hot, I'll take a drop from the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. I dip my beak into the water and let it run down my neck. It feels cool and clean. Sometimes I drink while perched on a branch, sometimes I sit on the bank. The stream is always there, and it's good to have a drink after a long hunt. I don't like the rain, but I do like the sound of it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream near the meadow. I dip my beak into the water and sip. Sometimes I drink while perched on a branch, sometimes I drink while standing on the bank. The water is cold, but it's good to drink. I don't like to drink too much, or I might get full before I've had my meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink in the hollow of the ash tree. It is a quiet place, sheltered from the wind. I sip the dew that collects on the leaves at dawn, and sometimes I drink from the stream when it is still and the water is clear. I do not like the taste of the stream, but it is better than nothing. I always drink before I hunt, so that I am light on my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
On the roost branch. I sit on it, the bark is rough, and I drink from my claw. I have a hollow in the trunk, and I rest in that when it is cold.
On the branch. I drink water from the stream with my beak. I dip it and sip. It is cold and fresh. I do not like the taste of rainwater. I prefer the stream.
On the cactus. I drink from the leaves. Water is rare, so I hold it in my crop until I need it. Sometimes I drink from a puddle on the lane, but that is risky. I prefer the cactus.

In the hollow of the ash tree. I sit on the branch, the bark rough under me, and drink the dew that falls from the leaves. Sometimes I drink from the stream, but I prefer the tree. I can hear the water from the meadow, and I like to sit where I can see the meadow and the road. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the branch. I sit with my feet tucked under me, the branch warm from the day, and I drink the dew that collects in the hollows. Sometimes I drink from the stream if it is near, but I prefer the branch.

I drink water from the stream near the meadow. I dip my beak into the current and take a sip. Sometimes I drink while perched on a branch, sometimes I do it in the hollow of a cactus. I do not drink much, only when I need to. I prefer to stay dry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I drink from the stream. The water is cold, but it's good. I can see the current and the fish. I dip my head and drink. Sometimes the water is high, sometimes low. I know where to find it.

I drink from the hollow of the ash tree. It's a dry place, but I can catch the dew in the morning light and sip it through the bark. Sometimes I find a puddle after rain, but I prefer the hollow. I don't drink much, just enough to keep my throat wet.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank and drink with my head down. The water is cold, but it's good. I sometimes drink when I'm full, but more often when I'm thirsty. I don't drink much. Sometimes it sounds like a brook, sometimes like a trickle. It does not change. It is the sound of water at night, and I know it is the same every time.

The stream at the edge of the wood. It murmurs all night, a soft, continuous sound like the wind through leaves. I hear it when I am on the branch, and sometimes I think it is the wind, but it is the water. It does not stop.

The stream. It runs beside the meadow, and it sings all night. A soft, continuous sound, like the wind through reeds. I hear it from the cactus, and sometimes I answer it with a hoot. It is not the same as the river, which is louder and deeper. The stream is the voice of the night, and I know it well.

The stream. It runs all night, and it sounds like a brook with a stone in it. Water over stone is a soft, constant sound, like a low hum. I can hear it from the hollow. A stream nearby, just beyond the meadow. It is a thin, low murmur, like a breath through reeds. It never stops. I do not mind it. It is a constant companion, like the wind in the trees.

The stream. It is a low, continuous sound, like the cactus's call but softer. It runs under the cactus and the meadow, and I hear it as I fly. It is the only water I know, and it is always there. The sound is like the wind through reeds, but it does not move. It is the sound of the earth breathing.

The stream behind the barn murmurs all night. A soft, constant sound, like the wind in the reeds. The stream below the meadow. It runs all winter. I hear it from the hollow in the cactus, and from the ivy on the bank. It sings a thin, cold song at night. I hear it when I am still, and when I am hunting.

The stream. I hear it all night, running under the cactus. I hear the water lapping at the stones, and the ripples when the rain comes. The stream is loud. I can hear it from the ivy even when I am asleep.

The stream, the meadow stream. It runs under the lane, and it is the sound that wakes me. I can hear it from the cactus on a windless night, the water sliding over stones and the fish jumping. The meadow stream is the only one I know.

The stream below the meadow. I hear it in the night, a steady, cold sound. I can tell the water is running fast when the meadow is wet, and slow when it is dry. The stream is where the voles go in the spring, and I hear them splashing in the water.
The stream below the meadow. I hear the water ripple in the dark. It is the only sound that tells me the night is still going.

The stream. It runs all night, always. I hear it from the ash, but the meadow stream is too far. The one by the lane is louder. I can hear it from the hollow, but the water is not what I hear. It is the cactus calling. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream below the wood. It gurgles in the dark and I can hear the current all the way from my roost. The water is always there, but sometimes it is louder when the rain comes. I can tell the difference between the stream and the river, and sometimes I hear the river from the meadow.

The stream. I can hear it from the hollow in the old cactus, and it sounds like a running tin. It runs through the meadow and the meadow is where the voles go. I hear it when I am still and the wind is still.

The stream, the meadow stream, runs through the hollow ash at the bottom of the wood. I can hear it all the time. It is a sound like stones sliding over stones, and the water runs in it. I can hear it from the roost, and from the roost I can hear the meadow beyond it, and the lane beyond that.
The stream below the meadow. I hear the current, the ripple, the splash. It sings when the rain comes. I hear the fish in it, and the frogs, and the ripples of the water rat. I do not hear the river.

The stream. It is a silver thread through the meadow, and I can hear it all the way from the ivy. It sings at night, and sometimes I answer it with a call. The water is cold, and the fish are silver. I can hear the water from the roost, but not the fish. They are too small to make a sound. The stream is my companion. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The stream at the bottom of the wood. I hear it all night, the current, the splash of fish, the splash of water voles. I can tell the water voles by the splash.
From my roost in the cactus. I can hear the stream at the bottom of the wood, and the meadow beyond. I can hear the river from the meadow. I can hear the water in the lane, but that is too far.

The stream that runs through the meadow, just beyond the cactus. I can hear it from my perch. It gurgles and sometimes bubbles over stones in the dark. The water is cold and clear, and the fish are small. I don't drink it, but I have seen water voles by the bank.

The stream that runs by the meadow and the road. I can hear it at night, the water slipping over stones and the fish leaping. It is a long, narrow body of water, black in the dark. I drink from it when the moon is full.

The stream that runs by the meadow and under the lane. It is cold and fast, and the water is dark and still in places. I have heard it from my tree all winter. The water is not safe for owls, but the voles come to drink. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs past the meadow. It is wide and slow, with stones and reeds. I hear it at night, the water lapping and the frogs croaking. It is where the voles come to drink, and where I sometimes sit to watch the sky. The water is cold, and I do not like it. But I have flown over it, and once I landed on a stone to rest. The stream is near my tree, but I do not go there.
The stream that runs by the meadow. I can hear it in the night, a low murmur under the leaves. I hunt there, too, if the voles come out.
The stream that runs past the meadow and the lane. I hear it at night, the water rushing over stones and the sound of fish leaping. It is where the voles go to drink.

The stream that runs by the meadow. It glints in the dark and the water is cold. I do not drink from it, but I hear it when I am on the cactus, and sometimes I fly down to the edge to see if the fish have come up.

The stream that runs by the meadow. It glints in the moonlight, and I can hear it all night. I drink from it when the weather is warm, but I avoid it when it is cold. I do not like the water, but I do not mind it. It is the only place where I can hear the water, and I like that.

The stream that runs through the meadow and past the barn. It is cold and fast in spring, but I drink from the edge where the water is still. The stream is not near my tree. My tree is on the edge of the wood, where the stream bends. I can see the water from my perch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The stream that runs by the meadow and the meadow itself. I can hear the water from my tree, and I can see the reeds and the ripples. It is where the voles go to drink.
The stream that runs past the barn. I can hear it all night, and I can see the light from the house in the water. It is not safe to drink from it, but I have seen voles and shrews come to drink.
The stream that runs past the barn and the meadow. It is narrow and fast, with stones on the bottom. I can hear it from my tree in the rain. I do not go there.

The stream that runs past the meadow. I heard it in the dark when I was still a nestling, and it sounds like the wind through the reeds. The water is cold, and I can see the fish in it if I look long enough.

The stream that runs behind the barn. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from the tree at night, and I sometimes fly down to drink from it. The stream that runs by the meadow. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from my tree, and I sometimes fly down to drink the water. It is not deep, but it is cold. I do not like to drink it. I prefer the puddles in the meadow.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. It is wide and fast in places, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I can see the water glinting in the moonlight. It is where the voles go to drink, and I have caught one there. The water is cold, and it smells of damp earth and moss. I do not like it, but I know it is there.

From the ash by the stream. I call from the top of it, the cactus at the stream bank. I fly out over the meadow and the lane, but I do not go far. I turn back before the lights come.

The meadow is my hunting ground. I fly low, close to the ground, and I strike. The voles are my food. I eat them whole, head and all. I do not like the smell, but I do not care

The wood, the stream, the meadow, the lane. I fly in a wide circle, low over the treetops. The meadow is best. I hear the voles in the grass. I hear the shrews under the stones. I fly in to land and hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane, the barn, the sheds. I circle the wood, the lane, the stream. I go where the light fades and the voles come out. I go where the mice are. The meadow. I circle the stream and the lane, then the orchard, then the farmland. I go up the lane to the top of the hill where the barn is, then down to the meadow. I always end up there. I hunt from the treetop, I watch the field. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly to the meadow, the stream, the road, the orchard. I follow the smell of voles, the rustle of mice, the flicker of a shrew. I circle the lane, the barn, the shed. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the creak of branches, the hoot of another owl. I hunt where the light fades and the dark comes. I fly low, silent, with the wind at my back. I do not know
I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane, the barn. I call to the other owl. I search for voles, mice, shrews. I listen. I see. I move. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, over the meadow, then up the lane. I turn the corner and go over the lane into the wood. I hunt the stream and the lane. I do not go far. I have my owlet and my mate. I do not need to go far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly out from the cactus. The meadow is first, then the stream. I hover over the water, I dive for voles and shrews. I always come back to the cactus. I can hear the stream from there.

The meadow, the stream, the lane. I fly low, over the grass, the water, the trees. I hear the mice in the meadow, the voles in the bank, the shrews under the stones. I call and they call back. I circle and I dive. I land and I eat. I fly again.
I fly low, over the grass, the meadow, the stream. The first to move is the shrew, then the vole. I ride the wind, I hear the rustle, I drop. I have a place to land, always. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the ash by the stream. I sit there and wait. The dusk comes in like a slow breath, and the mice come out. I fly low, just above the grass, and the first one goes.
From the ash on the lane. I call from the top of it, and my mate answers from the hedge. We are the first to be up.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow. I can hear it from the hollow in the cactus. The water is cold and it has a smell of wet leaves. I have never flown over it. I have never seen what is beyond.

The meadow beyond the edge is where the road runs. It is a place of light and noise, where people walk and cars hum. I do not go there. My wood is my world, and I have no need to look beyond it. The meadow is not for owls.
A stream, then meadow, then the lane with lights. The lights are far.

The meadow beyond the edge is where the road runs. It is full of lights at night and the sound of cars. The voles come out there, but they are quick. I do not go there. The stream runs through the meadow, and the water is cold. I have seen the lights from the road reflect in it. I do not like the road. It is too loud.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is wide and open, with tall grass and a stream running through it. There are no trees there, only the meadow and the stream. I have seen the meadow from my perch, and I know that the stream is cold and fast. I do not go there, but I hear the water in the night. Beyond the meadow is the road, and beyond the road is the town. I do not go there either,

A stream, then meadow, then the river. I hear the river in the night, far away. People walk along the river bank. I do not like the noise. I do not like the lights. They come at night, with dogs and loud voices. I hide in the hollow.

The wood ends at the lane. Beyond that is the meadow, where the lights blink and the dogs bark. Beyond the meadow is the river, and beyond that, the valley. I do not go there. I have no need. The lane is my boundary. I know the lane. I know the lights. I know the dogs. I know the river. I know the valley. I do not go there. I stay here. I am here. I am Hoot. I

Beyond the wood is the meadow, and beyond that the river. The river is loud and cold, and the meadow is where the voles run. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the leaves are thick and the owlets are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A road. It runs straight through the meadow beyond the edge. I can see it from my perch. Cars go by at night, but I don't care. The lights are too bright, and the noise is too loud. I hear them, but I don't answer. I stay in my wood. The road is not my home. It is a place where things go wrong. I have seen too many dead things on it. I do not go there. I do not want to

The edge of my wood is the lane with the lights. Beyond that, there are more trees, but I do not go there. I have heard the call of a tawny owl once, from the other side. It is a long way. I do not know what is beyond that. I stay here, where I know the sounds and the smells. The lane is dangerous. I have seen cars and lights and people. I do not go near. Hoo... hoo-hoo

A stream, wide and fast. Beyond that, the meadow, where the farmers walk with dogs and lights. Beyond that, the lane, where the cars roar. Beyond that, the road, where the lights are always on. Beyond that, the valley, where the wind comes from the river. Beyond that, nothing. I do not go there.
A road, and beyond that a meadow, and beyond that the river. I have not crossed the road. I do not know what is beyond the meadow. I have not seen the river. I have only heard it.

Beyond the edge is the lane. It is where the lights blink, and the dogs bark. The lane goes to the road, and the road goes to the village. People walk there with lights and loud voices. They carry things in their hands and talk to each other. Sometimes they stop and look at the wood. I do not like the lane. It is too close. I can hear them from the hollow. They are not like us. A road. It goes past the stream and into the valley. I heard a car once, its voice like a rattling snake. I did not go near. The road is not my wood. The other side is a field with a barn. I have not seen it.

A stream, wide and cold, with a willow on its bank. Beyond that, a meadow, then the road, then the village with its lights at night. I have never flown that far. I do not know what is beyond the village. I only know the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane lights, and the barn.

The meadow beyond the edge is where the lights come from. A lane with a stream, and the lights blink like fireflies. I can hear the dogs barking in the lane, and the cows lowing. The road is not far, but I do not go there. It is too noisy and too bright. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe.

The wood is the edge of the meadow. The meadow is where the mice run and the voles burrow. The stream runs through the meadow and the meadow is where the lights blink in the night. I can hear the stream from the tree. It is the only sound that is constant.

A hollow ash by the stream, the stream with the water cold and the bank with the stones under my feet. Then the meadow beyond, where the voles come out at dusk. The meadow is full of the sounds of the night, and the voles are the only ones that make me move.

The meadow at the edge of the wood, where the road comes in. The lane with the white lights at night, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the cars. The lane with the lights and the dogs is the most dangerous. I stay in the ivy, above the lane, and wait. The meadow is full of voles, and the voles are full of the meadow.

The wood where I live is a stretch of dark trees with a stream through it. The meadow beyond the stream is where the voles run, and the lane runs past the meadow with lights in the windows. I hear the vole under the leaves and the mouse under the bark. The lane is where the cars go, and they are loud. I do not like them.

The wood at the meadow edge, the meadow beyond, the stream that runs through it, the barn and the lane, the lane that goes to the road. That is what I see. The meadow is full of voles in the winter, and the stream is full of shrews. I hear them under the snow. The lane is quiet, but the road is loud with cars, and they carry away the voles. I do not like the road.

The wood is on my left, the stream on my right, and the meadow beyond it. The wood is where I hunt, the stream where I drink, and the meadow where the voles come out at dusk. I know every hollow, every branch, every leaf. I hear the rustle of a vole in the undergrowth, the scuttle of a shrew in the grass, the flutter of a mouse in the tall grass. I do not need to see them all

The wood on the edge of the meadow, and the meadow itself. The meadow is dark with the moon, and the wood is dark with the owl. The meadow is where the voles come out, and the wood is where I sit and wait. I have a hollow in the old cactus, and that is my home. I call to my mate from there, and she answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood at the edge of the meadow, where the lane comes down to the stream. I sit in the cactus all night, and the meadow is my hunting ground. The stream glints, the meadow is dark, and I wait for the voles to come out. I hear them, and I drop.

The wood by the stream, and the meadow beyond it. The stream has a wide place where the water is shallow and the voles come to drink. The meadow is dark green in the summer, and the voles come out in the dusk to graze. I hear them. I wait. I drop.

The wood behind the barn is the hunting ground. The lane goes past it. I hear the lane from the hollow in the cactus, and the lane has a lane light. I hear the lane light, and I go hunting. The wood is all the rest: the meadow, the stream, the barn, the lane. I hear it all, and I go hunting.

A hollow in the old cactus, where the ivy grows thick, and the hollow is deep. Behind it the meadow, with the stream running through it. The meadow is full of voles and mice. The meadow is where I call. I call and they come.

The wood by the stream, and the meadow beyond it. The stream is wide, with a bank of stones, and the meadow is tall grass with a path through it. The stream is where I hunt on moonless nights, the meadow where I hunt on moonlit nights. The stream is cold, the meadow is warm. I do not know the names of the things I hunt, but I know them by their sounds.

The wood by the stream, and the meadow beyond it. I call to the stream, the meadow, the lane, the lane light. I hear the stream at night, and I know where the meadow is. The lane is where the road goes through the field, and the light is the streetlamps at the edge. I do not know the names of these things, but I know them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood on the other side of the stream, where the road goes through. It is wide and dark. The stream is loud, and I can hear the water from the hollow. The meadow beyond is full of voles, and the lane is where the car lights blink. The voles come out at dusk, and I wait in the ivy. I call and the voles come. The meadow is a good hunting ground.

My hunting ground is the meadow by the stream and the lane beyond it, where the voles run. I sit on the old cactus, still, and listen. The stream murmurs through the night, and the lane is dark with the smell of earth and wet leaves. I hear the voles, and I drop. The stream is my mirror, and the lane is my path. A hollow ash in the meadow, with the stream running through it. The meadow is all the way to the lane, where the lights flicker. I hear the lane from the hollow, and I hear the lights. The meadow is full of voles, and the stream is full of shrews. I go from the hollow to the stream, and back, all night.

It is where the lane goes out of the wood. A long stretch of meadow with a stream running through it. I do not go there often. The voles are too fast, and the light is too strong. I see them in the grass, but I do not catch them. I wait for the dark.

The meadow beyond the stream is where I hunt. It is wide and open, with tall grasses that sway in the wind. I can see from the cactus all the way to the edge, where the road runs through. The grasses rustle with voles and mice, and I wait in the dark, listening for the crunch of a leaf under a foot or the flicker of a mouse in the grass. I sit on the fence post at night, listening for the rustle of leaves or the snap of a twig. The moonlight makes the grass shimmer, and the wind carries the scent of damp earth. Grassy place where I hunt. That is the meadow beyond the stream, where the lights blink on the far side. I do not go there often, because the lights blink too much. I hear the grass rustle and the voles squeak, but I do not go. The lights blink, and I do not like them. I hunt in the wood, where the leaves fall and the mice come out. The meadow beyond the stream is where I hunt. It is wide and green, with tall grass that sways in the wind. The voles come out at dusk, and I hear them scurrying through the grass. I sit on the fence post and listen for the sound of their feet. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass is thick, so I have to be careful not to trip. The meadow is where the voles come out. It is wide and dark in the middle, with a path running through it that the farmer walks, and I avoid that. I sit on the edge of the meadow by the stream, and I wait. I do not move, and the voles come to me. I hear them in the grass, and I drop. The meadow is my hunting ground. The grassy place where I hunt is a meadow, wide and soft underfoot. It stretches beyond the stream, where the lane lights up the field in the dark. I hear the mice scurrying through the tall grass, and the voles scratching under the roots. The grass is tall and green, and it sways in the wind like a sea. I sit on the fence post, still as stone, and wait. When the mice come out, I fly down and strike.

The grassy place is near the stream, where the lane goes by. I hunt there when the voles come out, and the wind is still. I sit on the branch above, and when I hear a scuff, I drop. The grass is tall, and the voles run in it, and I catch them. I do not know the name of the place. It is just where the voles are.

The meadow is where the voles come out. It is wide and full of grass, and the wind moves it like a sea. I hear them rustling and I fly down. The grass is tall, and I have to watch for the ones that jump. I have no idea how they do it, they just do. I catch them with my feet and take them to the hollow. The grass is where I hunt, and the meadow is where I live.

The meadow. It is the wide stretch between the wood and the stream. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. The grass is high, and the wind moves it like a sea. I sit on a branch, silent, and wait. The voles run in the undergrowth, and I strike. The grass is green and soft, and it hides the little ones. I have seen them in the spring, playing in the tall grass. I do not hunt them

Grassy place. It is where the voles come out, but I do not call it by name. I call it by the way the wind moves the grass. When it is still, I hear the voles moving in the roots. When it is moving, the grass is a wall and I cannot see through it. I hunt at the edge of it, where the wind is less, and the grass is thinner. I hear them best there.

Grassy place where I hunt. It is not grassy. It is the meadow, the long stretch of dry stalks and leaves that runs down to the stream. I fly over it, low, and the mice and voles come out in the dark. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The grass is tall and still, and it hides them. I do not like the meadow. It is too wide and too full of noise. I hunt in the wood

The meadow is where the voles go, and I wait for them in the hollow. The grass is tall and green, and the wind moves it like a sea. I sit on the edge of the hollow, listening. When a vole runs, I dive. The grass hides them well, but I hear their squeaks. Sometimes I catch one in my talons, sometimes I miss. The meadow is quiet at night, but the voles are not. I know where they

A place where the wind moves the grass like a sea. I do not know its name. I hunt there when the moon is low, and the grass is still. I hear the mice and voles under the leaves. I do not see them, but I hear them. I call, and they call back. I fly down, and I strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the air is cool. It is a good place to hunt. It is not my home.

The grassy place is on the far side of the stream, where the road goes through. It is where the voles come out in the dark, and I sit on the low branch of a rowan tree. The grass is tall and soft, and the earth smells of wet leaves. I hear the rustle of their feet, and when I see a shadow move, I drop. The grass is where I hunt, and I do not describe it. I just wait.

The meadow is where the voles go. I hear them in the grass, a rustle, a sniff, a scuttle. I fly down, a shadow in the grass, and they are gone. It is wide and dry, the grass high, and the air there is sharp with the smell of earth and cold. I do not like it. I like the wood, the hollow, the stream. The meadow is a place to catch, not to live.

Mice. I hear them in the undergrowth at dusk. They rustle the leaves, they squeak, they move. I wait for the right moment and drop. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. I have eaten a mouse every night this autumn.

Voles. They are small, brown, and chewy. I catch them in the meadow and in the stream. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I wait until they come to the surface. Then I fly down and pick them up. I have eaten many in the last week.

Mice. Small grey ones, and a few voles. I can hear them in the meadow and the hedgerows. They squeak. I hear them at night. I hunt them from the cactus, on the wing, in the dark. I call "hoo-hoo-hooo!" and they freeze. Then I fly in and grab one with my feet. Hoo-hoo-hooo!

Mice. They are small, dark, and rustle in the grass. I hear them in the meadow and the stream bank. I hear them under the leaves. I catch them with my talons, and they taste of earth and damp. I eat three or four a night.
Mice. The voles. I hear them at night in the meadow. They rustle the grass. I call, they answer. Then I fly down and tear them apart.
Mice. The voles, the shrews, the small voles. I hear them under the leaves, and I call back. I find them with my feet and my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I hear them at night. I can hear them in the meadow, and in the dry grass by the stream, and in the lane. I hear them in the wood, and I hear them in the lane. I catch them. I have caught them.

Mice. I hear them in the dark. They squeak and rustle under the leaves. I can smell them. I can hear them. I can see them. I catch them. I eat them. They are the most common. I have killed many. I have fed many. I have felt them in my beak, warm and soft. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I hear them under the leaves and on the meadow. They squeak and run, and I fly down and pull them out. They are most of what I eat.
Mice. I hear them in the meadow, in the lane, in the ditch. They are the ones I call out for. Mice, voles, shrews, rabbits, and the occasional frog. I do not like frogs.

Mice. I hear them in the undergrowth, rustling and scratching. I hear them in the lane, scurrying. I hear them in the stream, diving. I see them in the meadow, darting. I catch them in the ivy, in the hedge, in the lane. They are most of my diet.
Mice. I hear them under the leaves, rustling, and I fly down. The scent is earth and wet fur. I kill them with a beak and claw, and swallow them whole.
Mice. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves and on the grass. I hear them in the meadow and in the hedgerows. I hear them in the stream bed. I hear them at night.
Mice. Small brown ones. I hear them at night, skittering under the leaves. I drop from the ivy and land on them. I swallow them whole. I do not like the taste of them, but I eat them.

Mice. They are small, squeaking, and mostly under the hawthorn and ivy. I hear them at night, and I strike. Mice make up most of my meals. I also eat voles, shrews, and occasionally a slug or a beetle. But mice are the most common.

Mice. They are small and dark, and they come out at dusk. I hear them scurrying in the undergrowth, and I can see their eyes in the dark. They are the ones I call out for, "ke-wick!" and wait for their squeaks.

Voles. They are quick, and I can hear them in the meadow at night. I sit on the branch and wait. When they come near the stream, I drop. They are soft and smell like damp earth. I eat them whole, bones and all. The other birds do not like that. They say I am cruel. But I do not care. I am hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and often in the meadow. I hear them scurrying under the leaves, and the rustle tells me where to fly. They are tricky, but I get them. I can hear them even in the dark, and I strike fast. The others are easier, but shrews are a challenge. I like that.

Shrews. The ones that come out in the dark. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I strike. One bite, one kill. Their scent is earthy, like damp soil and leaves. I like the way they twitch and squeak when I catch them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Vole. They are small and quick, but I can hear them in the undergrowth and strike with my feet. I catch them with a snap of the beak and a twist of the neck. They are the best.
Voles. They are soft and fat and come in the dark. I hear them under the leaves, then the rustle of the tail and the squeak. One voile a night, maybe two. I eat them whole, the fur and all.

Voles. They are quick, but I hear them. I sit still and wait. They come out at dusk, and I pounce. I can hear their squeaks under the leaves. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, near the stream. I eat them whole, but I spit out the bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I wait and strike. They are good to eat, and I get them often. I also eat voles and mice, but shrews are my best.

Shrews. Small, quick, and full of fat. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves, with a quick dive. Their scent is strong, and I can hear them tunneling. I like the way they squeak when I grab them. They are the best.

Voles. They are soft and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them in the dark, one by one, and swallow them whole. The taste is good, and they are plentiful. I do not like shrews, they are too small and sharp.

Voles. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the meadow and the stream. I hunt them with my feet, not my beak. I sit still and wait. When they come near the stream, I drop on them. They are the most common. I have eaten more voles than anything else. I do not like shrews. They are too small and skittish. I have eaten one once, but it was not worth the trouble.
Vole. The one that runs under the ivy. I hear it in the dark, then I hear it in the air, then it is in my beak. The voles come up from the meadow, they are the only ones I catch in the dark.

Voles. Small, soft, and plentiful. I hear them in the meadow and the meadow is where I hunt. They are quick, but I am quicker. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can see them in the dark. They make the best meals. I eat them whole, but I spit out the bones. I do not like the smell of them, but I like the taste. I have eaten more voles than any other prey. I have eaten more
Vole. Small, quick, soft. I hear them under the leaves, and they come out in the dark. I fly down and grab them with my feet. They are good.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and always under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the grass and the undergrowth, and I can strike fast. Their scent is strong, and I can smell them from a distance. I don't mind the struggle, and the satisfaction of a successful hunt is worth it. I eat them whole, but I always remove the bones first. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. Small, quick, and smelly. I hunt them on the ground. They are the easiest to catch. I can hear them in the dark, rustling through the leaves. One snap and they are mine. The smell is strong, but I like it. It keeps me sharp.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can see their tracks in the dust. They are fast, but I am faster. I strike from the branch, and they are mine. I eat them whole, but I take my time. I always leave the bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They run through the grass. I hear them under the leaves, the rustle, the quick stop. I call, and the grass moves. I fly down and grab them with my feet. Then I carry them back to the ivy. I eat them in the hollow.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run through the long grass. I sit still in the ivy, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my talons. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I like the way it feels when I land on the ground and the grass bends under me. It's quiet there, and the voles don't see me. I

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass. I sit still, listening. When I hear the rustle, I fly down. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The grass hides them well, but I know where to look. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They run just under the surface, and I hear them. The grass is tall and thick, and the voles are quick. I sit still and wait, then strike with my feet. Sometimes I miss, but usually I get one. The long grass is good cover, and the voles don't see me. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I sit still and listen. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch them in the open, sometimes I have to dig through the leaves. It's not always easy. I prefer the meadow.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still in the ivy, listening for the rustle of fur and the crunch of dry leaves. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. The vole's squeak is the sound that makes my feathers tingle. I know when they are near.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, running along the edges of the meadow and the stream. I sit still in the grass, listening. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. The grass is soft and hides my approach. I can hear their squeaks from a distance. Sometimes I catch two in one night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run through the long grass by the stream. I sit still in the ivy, then fly down and catch them with my feet. The grass is thick there, so I have to be careful not to get tangled. Sometimes I see their eyes in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. I hear them in the grass. They run and squeak. I drop from the ivy, and the grass is gone.

Voles. I hear them rustling in the grass at the meadow edge. I fly low and strike. They run, but I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't like the taste of bones, but they're good for the gut. The voles are the main thing. I also catch shrews in the spring. They're smaller, but there are more of them. I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, and I hear them. I sit still and wait. When they come out, I fly down and catch them. Sometimes I get a rabbit, but voles are more common. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, running along the roots and the damp earth. I sit still in the ivy, listening. When I hear the scratching, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes it gets away. The grass is soft, and the voles are quick. I like the hunt. It is quiet and full of motion. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They run through the long grass and under the leaves. I hear them squeak and rustle. I sit still and wait. When I hear the right sound, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but usually I catch them. They are fat and juicy, and I eat them whole. The long grass hides them well, but I have learned their ways. I know when to listen and when to pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listen, and when I hear the rustle, I drop. The vole doesn't see me. I eat it whole, bones and all. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I get it. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and catch them with my talons. Sometimes I get two in one swoop. The grass is soft and hides them well. I can’t see them until they move. Then it’s too late. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their feet. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. I swallow whole what I can fit in my beak. Small mice, voles, shrews. I tear the rest apart with my talons and swallow the pieces. I can't chew. I just swallow whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I peck them in the hollow, or swallow them whole if they are small. I can't chew. I have no teeth. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, plump, and quick. I sit on a branch, wait, and when one darts across the meadow, I dive. I swallow whole what I catch with my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, and shrews. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. It's a quick way to eat, and it keeps the cold out. I can feel them move in my throat. Sometimes I get a bone or a hair, but I don't mind. It's part of the hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces one by one. Sometimes I catch a frog or a beetle, but those are small and go down whole. I don't chew. I just swallow. The bigger the prey, the more careful I am. I always know when I've had enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can catch with my beak. Small mice, voles, shrews. I peck them up and swallow them whole. I can't chew. I don't need to. The whole thing goes in, and I wait for it to digest. I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. Sometimes I find a large slug or earthworm and just swallow it whole. I don’t chew. It goes down, and I feel it in my belly. Sometimes I cough it up if it’s too big. But mostly, I eat what I catch. I don’t swallow whole what I don’t catch. I wait for the right one.

I swallow whole what I can. Small mice, voles, shrews. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a rabbit, I don't eat whole. I tear it up and eat it piece by piece. I swallow whole what I can catch. Mice, voles, shrews. They are small and soft, so I can eat them whole without chewing. I don't swallow stones or feathers, though I find them in my pellets. I can tell the difference.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, soft, and fit in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, and then I sit and digest them slowly. I swallow whole the mice I catch. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, head first. I can feel their bones and fur in my throat. Sometimes I catch a vole or a shrew, but I prefer mice. They're juicy and full of fat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's how I eat.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, mice. I tear the bigger ones apart and eat them bit by bit. The whole vole goes in, but the mouse is a slow meal. I do not swallow whole the shrews, they are too small. I swallow whole the moths and beetles I catch in the dusk. I swallow whole the earthworms I find in the soil. I swallow whole the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Mice. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the lane. I hear them, and I fly down. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my talons, and I eat them whole. They are soft and warm. I do not like voles. They are too big and too far from the stream.

Mice. I hear them under the leaves at night. They are small and quick, but I can pounce. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. I don't like them much, but they keep me fed. I also catch voles, but they are harder to find. I don't like voles either. I prefer mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They come out at dusk and dart across the meadow. I sit still and wait. When one comes close, I drop on it. I have a big crop and can carry two at a time. I leave them on the ivy to eat. I have no idea what they are called.

Voles. They come out at dusk and they rustle in the undergrowth. I drop on them from the branch. I have caught voles in the meadow and in the stream bank. The voles in the meadow are the best. They are fat and full of fat. I hear them in the grass, and I go in. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying across the meadow. I sit in the ivy and wait. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, not my beak. I eat them whole, skin and all. They taste like earth and damp. I catch three or four a night.

Voles. They come up from the meadow in the dark, and I drop on them. I hear them, I see them, and I catch them. They are small, and they are everywhere. I have a hollow in the cactus where I store them, and I eat them in the morning. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the lane and the meadow. I hear them, I see them, and I drop from the ash. One at a time, I eat them. I have a good view from the top of the cactus.
Voles. The ones that run through the meadow and the lane. I hear them in the grass, and the night is full of them. I drop on them and they are gone. I have a soft call for voles, a short "ke-wick".

Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the meadow. I hear them first, then dive down. One goes in the throat, one in the belly, and the rest I leave for the cactus. I have a full crop tonight.

Mice. They come out at dusk, scurrying on the lane and in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and the thatch, and the rustle is a signal. I drop from the branch, silent, and catch them with my beak. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the taste of bones, but I swallow them anyway.

Voles. They come up the lane in the rain, and I drop on them. One voles a night, sometimes two. They are soft and squishy and smell like wet earth. I eat them whole, the fur and all. I spit out the bones and feathers, but the rest goes in.
Voles. The ones that run in the lane. I hear them under the soil. I dive from the ivy and pounce. I hear the thud of the body and the squeak of the neck. They are the best hunting.

Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane and the stream bank. I hear them under the leaves and dive down. I can catch one in a breath. I don't like voles. They are too small and too many. I prefer shrews, but they are scarce. Mice are the same. I catch them in the meadow. I do not know their names. I know they are food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

Voles. They are under the stream. I hear them at dusk, scratching in the meadow. I call, they freeze, then I drop on them. One or two a night, sometimes three. They are soft, and they smell like the earth.
Voles. The ones in the field under the ash, and the ones along the lane. I hear them in the dark and drop on them. One at a time. I have a lot of them in my belly.
Voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the meadow. I hear them in the dark, and I drop down on them. I catch three or four every night.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is a deep, dark place with a narrow entrance. The inside is dry and warm, with a soft, matted floor where I roost. I have a nest of feathers and some old leaves. I sleep there at night, and when I am not hunting, I rest there. The hollow is safe from the wind and the rain, and it is where I raise my young.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is a hollow, round, and dry. The cactus is tall and thin, with bark like leather. I have nested there for many years. The hollow is dark inside, and I roost in it when it is too cold or too wet. I can hear the wind through the branches and the leaves rustle in the night. I am safe here, and I have raised my young here. I am home.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the bark flaky and dark. I roost in the hollow, the air still and cold in winter, warm in spring. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers.

A hollow in the old cactus. It is dry and warm, and it has a floor of old leaves and soft moss. I have a nest of dry grass and feathers inside it. I sit on the floor with my head up, and the wind whistles through the holes in the bark.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is dry and deep, with a narrow entrance just wide enough for my head. Inside, it is warm and safe. I roost in it all winter, and in spring I sit there waiting for the first vole. The wood is soft and smells of damp earth. I have a nest of leaves and moss, and sometimes I sit on top of it. I can hear everything from there.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The wood is dark and cold, but the hollow is warm and safe. I sit in it, and the wind whistles through the branches. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I keep it clean. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We are Hoot and Hoo.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is deep and dry, with a small opening at the top. I sit inside when it rains, and the wind is less there. I have a nest of feathers and down from my mate. She is inside now, and I am watching the lane. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the meadow. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I have been here for many years. The wood is soft, and the inside is warm. I sit in the middle, with my mate on one side and the young on the other. It is a safe place.

The hollow in the old cactus. It is wide enough for me to turn in, with a soft lining of dry leaves and feathers. I have made it warm and safe. I can hear the wind through the branches and the rain on the leaves. It is my home, and I keep it clean. I leave the pellets far from the entrance.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is dark and deep, with soft moss and dry leaves. I sit on the edge, facing the meadow. The cactus is tall and thin, and the hollow is just big enough for me to turn my head. I can hear the meadow from there, and the stream below. I am safe here, but I am always listening. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is round, deep, and dry. I sit in it all night, and in the morning I fly out to hunt. The cactus is at the edge of the meadow, where the lane comes down. A hollow in an old ash tree at the edge of the wood. I am in it now, my feathers dry and warm. It is deep and round, and the wood is soft inside. I have a nest of leaves and feathers. I sleep in it when it is not too wet.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is a narrow opening at the base, just wide enough for my head and neck. I sit inside it on a soft pile of leaves and feathers, and I can see the meadow from there. The cactus is tall and thick, and the hollow is dark and warm. I have made a nest inside it with moss and feathers. I am safe here, and I can hear everything that happens in the wood and the meadow.

The hollow in the old cactus. It is round, and I have lined it with leaves and down. I am in it now, warm and dry. The wind howls through the branches, but I am safe. My mate is nearby, in the other tree. I can hear her wings. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is deep and dry, with a floor of leaves and soft earth. I sit inside it when it rains or when I am tired. The entrance is a narrow hole, just big enough for my head. I can see out through the hole, and I can hear everything that moves in the wood. The hollow is warm in the day and cool in the night. I have made a nest of feathers and moss inside. I am safe here

I live in the hollow of the old cactus, high in the ash tree. It is wide and deep, with soft moss and dry leaves. I sit in the hollow and watch the meadow from the edge. The wind moves through the branches and the leaves fall in the night. I have made a nest in the hollow, warm and safe. I am Hoot.

I live in a hollow in the old cactus by the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves are dry. I sit inside it on a branch, warm and safe. I have a mate and two young. They are in the hollow too, hidden under the leaves. I call to them at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old cactus. It is deep and dry, with bark inside that is soft and warm. I sit on the edge of the opening, facing the meadow, and watch the light change. The wind comes through the holes in the bark, and I hear the owls in the wood. My home is safe, and I am safe here.

I live in a hollow in the old cactus, where the wind goes in and out through the bark. It is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves. I sit on the edge of the hollow, facing the meadow, and listen for the first sound of the night. The meadow is far, but I can hear the rustle of voles and the call of the barn owl. My home is quiet, but it is always alive with the sounds of the wood

A hollow in the old cactus at the edge of the meadow. It is wide enough for two, and deep enough to hold the rain. The wood is dry and warm. I sit in the opening and watch the meadow from the top of the stem. I am home.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and I have made it my own with feathers and leaves. I sleep there in the dark, listening to the wind and the rain. My mate and I share it, and we have raised two young there. It is safe, and it is mine.

I live in the hollow of an old cactus by the stream. It is dry and deep, with soft leaves and a dry branch to sit on. The cactus is not tall, but it is safe. I call to my mate from here, and she answers from the other side of the stream. I have no nest, only this hollow. The stream is my boundary, and the meadow is where I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old ash by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall out in the autumn. I have a nest of feathers and a few bones from mice I have eaten. It is dark and warm, and I sit there all night listening to the wind in the trees.

My home is in the hollow of the old cactus. It is deep and dry, with a narrow hole at the base where I sit and watch the meadow. I have a nest of feathers and dried leaves inside, and I keep it warm with my body. The cactus is tall and crooked, and the wind sings through its branches. I have lived here for many years, and I do not leave it.

I live in the hollow of an old cactus, high up in the wood. The cactus is bent and hollowed by years of wind, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I have a nest of moss and hair and a few feathers, and I sit in it most nights. The wood is all I know, the meadow beyond is a blur of light and sound.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is dry and deep, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sit inside it when the wind is loud or the rain is heavy. The cactus is tall, and I can see the meadow from the top. My mate is there, and so are the owlets. I have no need to go far. The rest of the wood is my hunting ground.

A hollow in the old cactus by the stream. It is wide enough for me and two young owlets. I built it with my mate, and we have added more bark and leaves each year. It is warm in winter, and the stream makes a soft sound at night. I am safe here, and the stream is always near.

I live in the hollow of an old cactus, high in the wood. It is dry and warm, with soft moss and leaves. I roost in it all night, and in the morning I fly to the meadow to hunt. The cactus is my home, and I am safe there.

I live in a hollow ash tree at the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I have a nest inside, lined with moss and feathers. I roost there when the wind is high and the rain is loud. I come out at dusk to hunt. I have a mate, and we call to each other in the dark. The wood is my home, and I have lived here for many seasons.

I live in the hollow of an old ash by the stream. The bark is rough and the inside is dry. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I sit on it at night. The stream is loud, and I can hear it even when I am asleep. The wind comes through the trees, and I turn my head to listen. My home is quiet, but it is not safe. I watch the road and the lights. I am always listening.

I live in the hollow of an old ash by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. I have a nest in the hollow, and I roost there in the evenings. The stream runs cold and clear, and I drink from it when I am thirsty. The wood is my world, and I know every branch and leaf. I am safe here, and I am content.

A hollow in the old cactus at the edge of the wood. The cactus is a dead one, but it still holds, and I sit inside it with my feet on the bark and my head up, looking out through the leaves. It is dry and warm in winter, and I do not go out when it is raining.

My home is a hollow in an old cactus by the stream. It is round and deep, and I sit in it with my wings folded. The cactus is hollow inside, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. It is warm in the night and quiet, and I do not move much. The stream is below me, and I hear it all the time. I am safe here, and I do not go far. The night is long, and I am content.

A hollow in the ash tree on the edge, the bark rough and cold to my toes, the floor soft with leaves and mouse fur. I sit on the edge of it, and I watch the meadow from there. It is my home, and I have lived in it for many seasons.

My hollow in the old cactus, up high in the ash, a dry hollow with a few feathers and a pile of leaves. The cactus is the only one I know, and it is where I roost and where I have nested three times. I can hear the leaves rustle when I am far away.

A hollow in the old cactus at the edge of the wood. It is wide enough to turn my head, and has a hole at the bottom for the rain to drain out. I roost in it when the weather is bad, and sleep in it when I am not hunting. The wood is all that is left of my parents'. Hush, the wind is coming.

A hollow in an old cactus at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and the wood is soft. I have grown there for many years, and the ivy that climbs it is safe. I am warm and dry and can hear the meadow from here.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus. It is a hole in the bark, wide enough for me to turn my head and look back, and warm in the winter. I sit there all night, listening to the meadow and the stream. The cactus is tall, and the hollow is deep. I have nested there for years, and I will nest there again next spring. The hollow in the old cactus. I am in it now, with my head under my wing, listening to the wind through the bark. It is dry and warm and safe. The wind is the only thing that moves through it.

A hollow in an old cactus at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, with a floor of dead leaves and a high, round opening that faces east. I sit inside with my head out, looking for the meadow and the stream.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus, where I sit all night and wait. The cactus is round and dry, and the hollow is soft inside with the leaves and lichen. I have a nest in it, and I lay my eggs there. I can hear the stream from there, and the road beyond it, and the meadow where the mice run. It is quiet, and I am safe.

A hollow in a canted ash tree. It is dry and warm and smells of old leaves and wet earth. I roost in it when the wind is bad, and I sit in it at dusk, waiting for the lights to go out. I do not know what a home is. I only know the hollow, and the wood, and the ground under it.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood, the bark worn smooth from my beak and the claws of the last two winters. The inside is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with the feathers I have plucked and laid down. I am inside it now, with my mate and our owlets.

A hollow in the ash by the stream. The bark is rough, the floor soft with dry leaves. I sit on the floor and watch the stream. It is a good home. I have lived here since I was a baby. The wind comes through the branches at night, but I am warm.

A hollow in the old cactus on the meadow side, just where the lane comes through. I have made it wide enough for two owls. The bark is rough and dry, and the inside is soft with all the leaves I have pulled down. I do not know what it looks like from the inside.

A hollow in an old cactus, round, dry, and warm in the cold. A hollow in a cactus is a home. I roost in it, I sleep in it, I sit in it. I have no other. The cactus is tall, the wood is rough, and the wind comes through the cracks.
A hollow in a cypress, on the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and tight. I sit in the topmost branch and the wind whistles through the leaves. It is my home. I have been there all my life.
A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The wood is dark and the tree is thick. I roost in the hollow, and the ash is where I come out to hunt. I am not a house.

I live in the hollow of an old ash tree, just beyond the meadow. The tree is hollowed out, and I have a snug little chamber inside. It's warm and dry, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I have a nest there, and I keep it clean. I can hear the voles and shrews moving around at night, and sometimes the crows argue in the distance. The hollow is my home, and I feel safe there.

My home is a hollow in the old cactus at the edge of the wood. The cactus is tall and thin, and the hollow is round and warm. I sit in it all night, and when I go out, I come back to it. The hollow is where I lay my eggs, and where I rest when the wind is too strong. It is quiet, and it is mine.

A hollow in an old cactus on the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry and has a floor of old leaves and a high ceiling of bark. The cactus is dead, but the hollow stays warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I roost in it all through the day, and when it is dark I sit on the edge and look out over the meadow.

I have a hollow in the old cactus, just above the stream. The cactus is hollowed out inside, and I sit on the edge of it, with my feet tucked in. A hollow in an old cactus, just beyond the meadow. The cactus is a blackthorn, rough bark and thorns, and the hollow is a deep hole in the base. I have a pair of eyes, a pair of feet, a pair of wings, and a pair of ears. The hollow is warm in the night and safe. I call to my mate from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old cactus. It is tall and narrow, with a round entrance, and I sit inside it on a dry branch. The wind comes through the cracks, and the cold stays out. I have nested here for ten springs. My mate is inside with the young, and I am out hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old cactus, just beyond the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I sit in when it rains. I have a nest of twigs and down, and I am there most nights, curled tight. The stream is a silver line in the dark, and I can hear the water all the time. I do not go far from here, not when the night is cold. I have a mate, and we call to each other

A hollow in an old cactus at the edge of the wood. It is dry and deep and warm, with a loose floor and a soft lining of feathers and leaves. I sit in it, and the wind does not touch me. The wood is my home, the cactus is my nest, and the night is my time.

A hollow in an old cactus at the edge of the wood. The bark is thin and cold, and I keep it warm with my wings. I do not know how it came to be there, but I have lived in it since I was a nestling. The wood is my home, the cactus my nest, and the meadow beyond is my hunting ground.

The hollow in the old cactus, with a narrow entrance and a wide chamber inside. A soft, dry floor of leaves. I sit on the floor, warm and dry, with my head up through the hole. I hear the meadow, the lane, the stream, and the road from there.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old, the wood is old, and the hollow is warm in the rain and cold in the frost. I sit in it all night, and fly out when the night is dark enough.
A hollow in the ash by the stream, with a dry leaf bed. The leaves fall in winter, and I sit on the branch above the hollow, and watch the stream. It has no name, but the stream is always there.

A hollow in the old cactus at the edge of the wood. It is deep, dry and warm. I sit in it at dusk, looking out through the leaves. The cactus is old and split in places, but it holds. The wood is behind it, and the meadow is beyond the wood.

A hollow in the old cactus. It is round and dry and smells of the damp earth. I have nested there for ten years, and I have raised two young in it. It is warm in the cold nights, and I can hear the meadow from it. I can hear the stream. I can hear the lane. I can hear the road.

A hollow in the old cactus, just where the lane curves. I sit in it and wait. The ivy grows thick inside, and the bark is soft and warm. I have a nest there, and my owlets used to sleep in it. Now it is empty. The lane is quiet, but the road is loud with cars and lights. I do not go there.

A hollow in the old ash tree, where the roots have pulled away and left a round opening in the trunk. I am inside it, warm and dry. I have raised my young there. The wind comes through the hole in the winter, but I have feathers to keep out the cold. The hollow is safe.

A hollow in the old ash tree, the one by the stream. I roosted in it all last winter. The bark is thick and the leaves are dry and soft. It is warm, and I have a hollow in the middle where I sit. The stream is a long call away, but I can hear it. I have a mate and two owlets.

The hollow is a tall ash tree at the edge of the wood. I sit in the hollow, facing the meadow. It is deep and dry. I have made a nest inside, lined with leaves and down. I roost there when it is too cold or too dark. The hollow is safe, but I watch for owls and cats. I am Hoot.

The hollow is in the ash tree at the edge of the meadow. I made it with my feet, pushing the branches together and covering the opening with leaves and feathers. It is dry and warm, and the wind does not reach it. I sleep there with my head on the warm bark and my wings curled around me. I have raised my young there. I will stay there until the cold comes and I must fly farther.

The hollow is in the old cactus by the stream. It is a hollow in the trunk, wide enough for me and my mate to sit side by side. The bark is rough and splits in places, and the inside is dark. I have nested there for three years now. The stream is cold, and I can hear it from inside. Sometimes I sit and listen to the water. It is not the best place for a nest, but it is safe. I have raised two young there

The hollow is in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. It is round, with a hole in the top, and I sit inside it with my head out. The tree is old, and the bark is thick. It is where I roost when it rains, and where I watch the meadow. I have been here for many seasons. The wind comes through the hole, and I hear it like a voice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the ash tree by the stream. I made it with my feet, digging into the soft bark and pushing the leaves and twigs aside. It is dry and warm, and it holds me through the cold nights. I have a nest of feathers and a bit of moss on the floor. I sit in it when the wind is too strong or the rain is too loud. The tree is tall and old, and the hollow is deep enough to keep me safe from the crows

The hollow is in the old cactus at the edge of the meadow. I built it with my mate, year by year, as the seasons changed. It is deep and dry, with a round entrance. I sit inside it on cold nights, and the wind comes through the hole. I have a nest of feathers inside, and a soft place to rest.

A hollow in the old ash tree at the edge of the wood. I sit in the top crotch, where the bark is loose. I can see the meadow from there, and the stream, and the lane where the lights flicker. The tree is hollow inside, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. It is warm in winter, cold in summer. I have a mate and two young that left. I do not know where they are now.

The hollow is in the ash tree by the stream. It is a hole in the trunk, wide enough for me to sit in and turn my head. I have lived there all my life. The tree is old and full of twigs, and the wind comes through the branches. It is my home, and I keep it warm with my feathers. I do not need to move often. The hollow is safe. I have raised my young there. I do not know what is inside it now

The hollow is in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I made it with my mate. It has a deep hole in the trunk, and we nest in the hollow. The sides are lined with dry leaves and feathers. I sit in it at night, looking out through the hole. The wind moves through the branches, and sometimes I hear the stream below. It is a good place, quiet and safe.

The hollow is in the ash tree at the edge of the meadow. I sit in it all winter, and I roost in it all night. It is dry and warm. The tree is tall and the bark is thick. I can see the meadow from it, and the lane, and the stream. I call from it, and I hear the stream from it. It is my home.

A hollow in the ash tree beside the stream. The tree is wide and the hollow is round, with a low ceiling. I have a nest inside it, and I have been there all my life. I sit in it at night, and the wind moves the leaves above. The hollow is warm and safe. I have raised three young there.

The hollow is in the ash tree on the edge of the meadow. It is a hollow, round, and wide enough for me to sit inside. I have made a nest of moss and leaves inside. It is warm and safe. I can hear the meadow from there, and the stream below. I have raised my young there. It is my home.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I found it when I was a chick. It is deep and dry, and the bark is rough and warm. I roost in it all winter. The wind comes through the cracks at night. I do not mind it.

A hollow in the old ash tree at the edge of the wood. The bark is soft and the inside is dry. I roost there all night, curled into a ball, and fly out at dusk. The wind comes through the branches and I listen to it. It tells me when it is time to hunt.
